opus-5.5.text:
I think there are a few layers to it. The first is that reinforcement learning is fundamentally a harder problem than supervised learning. In supervised learning you have a fixed dataset and a stationary target. In RL, the data distribution depends on your own policy, so as the agent learns, the thing it's learning from shifts underneath it. You're chasing a moving target, and small changes early on can compound into very different outcomes later.

On top of that, many of our algorithms were developed with a lot of implicit tuning to specific benchmarks. People take a method, adjust hyperparameters, network sizes, and implementation details until it works on Atari or MuJoCo, and then the paper reports that it works. But much of the performance lives in those details: how you normalize advantages, how you clip, learning rate schedules, and so on. When you move to a new environment, all that hidden tuning no longer applies, and the algorithm falls over.

There's also an evaluation problem. RL experiments have historically been expensive, so people ran a handful of seeds, and with high variance you can convince yourself something works when you've just been lucky. That's partly why I've been excited about running environments and agents end to end on accelerators. When you can train thousands of agents in parallel on a GPU, you can actually measure the variance, sweep hyperparameters properly, and see how robust a method really is.

More philosophically, I think it shows that many of our algorithms are hand-designed heuristics that happen to work in some regimes. That motivates meta-learning: rather than relying on human intuition to design the update rule, can we learn algorithms that are robust across a distribution of environments? If brittleness comes from overfitting our designs to a few benchmarks, part of the answer is to search more broadly and evaluate more honestly.

r001.rationale: It says algorithms are implicitly tuned to specific benchmarks and that hidden tuning fails to transfer to new environments.

r002.rationale: It explains that running many agents in parallel enables broader sweeps and more reliable robustness evaluation, supporting development of more robust methods.

r003.rationale: It describes meta-learning as learning update rules across environments, but does not characterize researchers’ own search for generalizing methods as meta-learning.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the brittleness comes from a few places, and they're kind of compounding.

The first is that RL is fundamentally a feedback loop. In supervised learning your data is fixed, so if your optimizer is a bit off you still converge to something reasonable. In RL the policy generates the data it learns from, so any small error gets fed back in. You explore the wrong region, you collect bad data, you update in the wrong direction, and now you explore an even worse region. Small mistakes don't average out, they compound. That's why you see these runs where one seed works beautifully and another seed with the exact same hyperparameters just collapses.

The second thing is that we've been tuning algorithms to benchmarks rather than understanding them. A lot of what we think of as "the algorithm" in something like PPO is actually a pile of implementation details, the clipping, the advantage normalisation, the way you handle the value function, and those details were found by trial and error on a handful of environments. So of course when you move to a new domain, the thing that was holding everything together isn't the theory, it's a bunch of heuristics that happened to work on Atari or MuJoCo.

And the third piece, which I think is underappreciated, is that we've massively underinvested in the evaluation side. We train on the same environments we test on, we report best-of-N seeds, and we treat a single learning curve as evidence. If you only ever look at the mean reward on the training distribution you can't even see the brittleness until you deploy somewhere new.

That's actually part of why I got excited about things like learned optimisers and meta-learning the RL algorithm itself, and about environments like Procgen and open-ended settings where you're forced to generalise. If you can't overfit to a fixed benchmark, you have to actually discover something robust. And the honest answer is we're still pretty early on that. A lot of what works today in RL, at scale, works because people threw enormous compute and careful engineering at it, not because the algorithms themselves are stable.

r001.rationale: It says algorithms are tuned on benchmarks and that details were found by trial and error on a handful of environments.

r002.rationale: It discusses generalization-focused environments, but does not say faster experimentation enables more robust methods.

r003.rationale: It mentions meta-learning the RL algorithm itself, but does not characterize researchers’ search for generalizing methods as meta-learning by the researchers.

astra-6.text:
I think part of it is that, in reinforcement learning, the learning process changes the data you get. You update the policy, that changes which states you visit, and now you’re learning from a different distribution. So a small error can feed back into the system: it changes your behaviour, which changes your experience, which can reinforce that error.

And you’re often learning from a fairly weak signal. If an action pays off a thousand steps later, figuring out which decisions were responsible is difficult. You combine that with function approximation, exploration, and bootstrapping—using your own predictions as targets—and you have several interacting sources of instability.

There’s also a methodological issue. If we tune an algorithm very carefully on a small set of environments, we can end up with something that looks robust in those environments but is sensitive to choices we haven’t really understood. I think the challenge is to understand which parts of the learning process make it reliable, rather than just finding a configuration that works.

r001.rationale: The response says careful tuning on a small set of environments can make an algorithm appear robust there while leaving it sensitive elsewhere, linking narrow environment optimization to brittleness.

r002.rationale: It does not identify faster experimentation as enabling more robust reinforcement learning methods.

r003.rationale: It does not characterize researchers’ search for generalizing methods as meta-learning.

sol-6.1.text:
I think part of the problem is that in reinforcement learning, the data distribution depends on the policy you’re learning. So when you update the policy, you’re also changing the data you’re going to collect. A small mistake can feed back into the learning process: you get a slightly worse policy, that policy collects less useful data, and now it’s harder to recover.

And you’re often learning several things at once. You’re learning a value function, using that to improve a policy, and relying on the policy to explore. Those components can compensate for one another for a while, so things look fine, and then suddenly the whole process becomes unstable.

I’d also distinguish between getting something to work on a particular benchmark and having an algorithm that reliably works when you change the environment, the reward scale, or the hyperparameters. We’ve become quite good at the first. The second requires understanding which assumptions make the learning process stable, and how to notice when those assumptions stop holding.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts benchmark-specific success with reliability across changed environments, but attributes brittleness to policy-dependent data and interacting learning components, not to optimizing on a narrow set of environments.

r002.rationale: It does not identify faster experimentation as enabling more robust methods.

r003.rationale: It does not characterize researchers’ search for generalizing methods as meta-learning by the researchers.
